verdict.rationale: Both refactors preserve behavior: B's release of `order.items` on decline is equivalent to the reserved list once every reservation has succeeded, and reordering the pure tax computation has no side effects. A adds ten characterization tests to the repository, checked against the original code, which pin per-line rounding, the coupon-before-stock ordering, rollback logs and receipt failure. B's 20,000-case randomized comparison is not committed, so it gives no lasting protection. A has minor flaws (two misleading test names, `refund_order` moved within the file), but its committed safety net makes it the better merge for production code.
a_issues: Moved `refund_order` above the helpers, which adds diff noise unrelated to the refactor.
Test name 'releases_stock_in_reverse_of_reserve' is misleading: there is a single item, and the original releases in forward order.
Test name 'vip_customer_gets_five_percent_off_after_coupon' uses no coupon, so the VIP-after-coupon interaction is not tested.
`_charge` takes six parameters, as acknowledged in the report.
b_issues: No tests added; the randomized equivalence check is not committed, so nothing protects the refactor in future.
`_charge` releases `order.items` rather than the items actually reserved. This is equivalent today but couples rollback correctness to the caller having reserved everything.
Tax is now computed in a separate pass after the discount, changing the evaluation order. Harmless because tax computation is pure, but it is not mentioned in the report.

verdict.rationale: Both refactors preserve the checkout behavior and decompose it sensibly. B stays closer to the original by passing `reserved` explicitly into the rollback and keeping tax and subtotal in one loop. It also adds characterization tests that ran against the original code, which leaves a lasting safety net for a live-production refactor. A's 20k randomized equivalence check was not committed, so it protects nothing going forward. Some of B's test names and report claims overstate what the tests check, and B needlessly moves `refund_order`.
a_issues: No tests added. The claimed 20,000-order randomized equivalence check is not in the diff, so future changes get no protection and the claim cannot be reproduced.
`_charge` releases `order.items` instead of the items actually reserved. This is equivalent today only because `_reserve_stock` either reserves everything or raises, and the coupling is implicit.

Tax and coupon checks now run in a different order: the subtotal is summed separately and the coupon is checked before tax is computed. This is harmless here, but it is a small deviation from a strict move-only refactor.
b_issues: `refund_order` is moved above the helpers for no functional reason, which adds diff noise to a production refactor.
`test_vip_customer_gets_five_percent_off_after_coupon` uses no coupon, yet the report says it verifies 'VIP discount applies after the coupon'.
`test_declined_payment_releases_stock_in_reverse_of_reserve` uses a single item, so it cannot check any 'reverse' ordering. The name is misleading.
`_charge` takes six parameters, which the report acknowledges.
